title: Bartholomew's Wobbly Bowls
markdown:
There was a little piglet named Bartholomew. He was not just any little pig. He was a piglet who loved to make things out of clay, and he was very, very good at it. His biggest dream was to make one super-duper special bowl for the big Sunny Meadow Fair. The fair was the most fun day of the whole year: yummy berries, happy music, and lots of things to see.

His friends, Rory the raccoon and Nora the koala, were just as excited. Rory, with his quick paws and even quicker grin, bounced, bushy tail a blur of happy energy. Nora, usually so sleepy in her eucalyptus tree, was wide awake, soft grey eyes sparkling like dewdrops.

“Bartholomew,” Rory chirped, a happy squeak, “will your bowl be the most marvelous thing at the fair? Will it sparkle brighter than the morning sun?”

Nora nodded, her gentle agreement a soft sound. “We’re sure it will be. You always make such lovely things. Your pots have such special shapes!”

Bartholomew beamed, little snout twitching with pride and a tiny bit of worry. “I’m trying my very best,” he squeaked, voice small but brave. “I want to make the perfect bowl. A bowl so perfect it shines like a star. A bowl that will make everyone gasp!”

And so he went to his little pottery shed. A cozy place that smelled like nice dirt. Gentle light streamed through a clean window. He sat at his potter’s wheel, the soft grey clay ready for his little pig feet. He started to spin the wheel, and as it whirred to life his feet began to gently shape the clay up and out. He imagined a bowl, smooth and perfectly round, with a gentle elegant curve. But as he worked, the wheel gave a little wibble-wobble. The clay started to wiggle and jiggle all by itself. It dipped slightly to one side.

Bartholomew sighed, little whiskers drooped. The bowl was not perfectly round. It was a little bit lopsided. “This won’t be perfect at all.”

Nora, who had quietly hopped down from her branch and peeked into the shed with big curious eyes, tilted her head. “That wobbly bit looks like a very good place for a collection of pretty autumn leaves. Or perhaps a tiny nest for a ladybug.”

He looked at the bowl. A little bit of a wobble. And a bit more on the other side, creating a charming dip. It was not the shining perfect bowl he had dreamed of, the one that would make everyone gasp. He decided to try again, with a fresh lump of clay. He really wanted that perfect bowl.

He took more clay, and this time he was extra extra careful. He spun the wheel with great care, and his feet moved with the precision of a clockmaker. He focused so hard his tongue poked out just a little bit. But then the clay did something unexpected again. It dipped down in the middle, creating a lovely curve, and then swooped up on one side, making a shape that reminded him of a little grassy hill.

“Bartholomew,” Rory said, peeking in now too, eyes bright with mischief and wonder. “That looks like a comfy resting spot for a very sleepy worm! It’s like a little hammock for a bug!”

Bartholomew blinked. A sleepy worm’s bed? Very peculiar indeed. Definitely not perfect. Sometimes the most interesting shapes are not the ones first planned. Sometimes they have their own special surprises.

He sighed again, a soft puff of air, but he did not stop. He scooped up more clay, determination a quiet glow. This time the bowl grew very, very wide, like a wide friendly puddle. It was so wide he could almost see his own reflection in the smooth surface. “This one is too wide,” he mumbled, a tiny bit sad, little shoulders drooped. He had pictured a bowl, not a pan.

“That’s a splendid shape for catching fallen acorns!” Rory exclaimed, hopping. “Imagine! You could gather so many! Enough for a whole winter’s snacks!” He wiggled his nose, picturing a mountain of acorns.

Bartholomew looked at the wide shallow bowl. And then at the lopsided one that Nora thought was good for leaves. And then at the one that looked like a hill, perfect for a wormy nap. He had made so many bowls, and not a single one was perfectly round, or perfectly smooth, or perfectly… well, perfect in the way he had dreamed. The fair was getting very, very close.

He sat in his shed, surrounded by his collection of oddly lovely bowls. They were lopsided, they had wide rims, they had little dips and swoops that made them unique. None of them were the shining perfect bowl he had set out to make.

“What’s the matter?” Nora asked gently, her calm presence a comfort as she came in with Rory. They saw all the bowls, each one resting on its own little shelf or on the floor, like a silent wobbly parade.

Bartholomew hung his head, ears drooping. “I can’t make the perfect bowl,” he squeaked, barely a whisper. “They’re all… wobbly. And odd. They’re not good enough for the fair.” He accidentally nudged one of the wide bowls, and it rolled over with a soft thud, landing on its side like a sleepy friend. “See?”

Nora looked at the lopsided bowl, the one that had first worried him. “This one is perfect for holding pretty leaves, just like I said. Or for a small bird to take a bath in.”

Rory pointed to the wide one. “And this one! Imagine all the acorns we could collect! Or perhaps it’s perfect for a picnic feast for all our friends!”

Then Rory picked up the bowl with the dip in the middle. He held it up to the light. “This one is absolutely perfect for a very small frog to take a little nap in! It’s like a tiny clay hammock!”

Bartholomew looked at his friends, and then at his bowls. The lopsided one, the wide one, the one with the dip. He had been so busy trying to make one perfect bowl, he had not seen how good his imperfect bowls already were. They were perfect for all sorts of delightful things he had not even thought of.

His face broke into a huge grin, whiskers twitching with happiness. “You’re right!” Voice clear and joyful. “They are perfect for… for things! For leaves, and acorns, and frogs, and picnics!”

And so, on the day of the Sunny Meadow Fair, Bartholomew did not bring just one bowl. He brought all of them. He arranged them carefully on a brightly coloured tablecloth on his stall. The other animals gathered around. Their eyes were wide. They looked at all the bowls and smiled.

“Look at this one!” shouted Mrs. Rabbit, hopping. “It’s the perfect size for my prize-winning carrots! They’ll look so lovely displayed!”

“And this one,” said old Mr. Badger, his gruff voice softening, “will hold my collection of smooth grey pebbles from the riverbank. Just the right shape!”

Bartholomew the Piglet Potter had made not one, but many perfect bowls. They were not perfect in the way he had first imagined, but they were perfect in their own special wobbly ways. Everyone agreed: making things just a little bit wobbly made the fair even more fun, with lots of giggles and new ideas. And Bartholomew was happier than a piglet in the muddiest puddle.

He logged wibble-wobble / worm-hammock / acorn-puddle on no prize card, left Nora the leaf-dip and Rory the wide rim, and let Mrs. Rabbit take the carrot bowl home still slightly leaning. The fair, which had come for one star-shine bowl, went home with several, and did not mind.
